best_architecture: Adopt MCP (Model Context Protocol) stdio transport as the polyglot bridge: each skill is a separate child-process MCP server that the host (Local-Claw nervous system) spawns and speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 to over stdin/stdout. This is the strongest pattern for a TS+Python+Rust skill mesh and is exactly how Local-Claw is already specced. Key design decisions, in priority order: (1) PROTOCOL AS CONTRACT, NOT ABI. MCP standardizes tool discovery (tools/list), invocation (tools/call), and JSON Schema input/output schemas over JSON-RPC 2.0 (the design is explicitly modeled on the Language Server Protocol). This makes language a pure implementation detail — a Rust skill and a Python skill are indistinguishable to the host because both expose the same JSON-RPC surface. Use each official SDK's native schema mechanism (Zod/Standard Schema in TS, Pydantic in Python, serde + schemars in Rust) and let it EMIT JSON Schema; never hand-author schemas, and never share a binary ABI across languages. (2) PROCESS ISOLATION OVER PLUGIN-IN-HOST. Running each skill as its own subprocess (vs. loading it into the host's address space like a classic dylib/plugin) gives crash isolation (a panicking Rust skill or a segfaulting native dep cannot take down the agent loop), independent dependency trees (no Python venv vs node_modules vs cargo conflicts), per-skill resource limits, and trivial polyglot support. The cost is per-call IPC serialization latency and process-spawn overhead — mitigate by keeping skill servers warm/long-lived (one persistent subprocess per skill, reused across calls) rather than spawning per invocation. This trade-off (isolation + polyglot vs. raw speed) is the central architectural call and process isolation is correct for an autonomous agent that loads untrusted-ish, heterogeneous skills. (3) SKILL DISCOVERY = MANIFEST FILE + REGISTRY, not blind filesystem scan. Each skill ships a small manifest (name, version, language, executable/command + args, env, declared capabilities) that the host reads to build a registry; MCP itself then provides runtime capability discovery via tools/list once the subprocess is launched. This two-tier model (static manifest for spawn config -> dynamic tools/list for actual tool schemas) mirrors the official modelcontextprotocol/registry (RESTful catalog over MongoDB) and the GitHub MCP Registry, and avoids fragile path-convention scanning. A filesystem scan can be a fallback to auto-populate the registry, but the manifest is the source of truth. (4) SECOND-TIER SANDBOX FOR UNTRUSTED RUST/COMPUTE SKILLS: WASM Component Model + WIT. For skills that need stronger sandboxing than OS process isolation (capability-based security, deterministic resource caps, portable single-artifact distribution), compile Rust skills to WASI Preview 2 components described by WIT interfaces and run them in Wasmtime, or use Extism (Wasmtime-based cross-language plugin framework) as a higher-level shim. This is a complementary inner layer: the skill is still presented to the agent as an MCP server, but the MCP server internally executes a WASM component (see hyper-mcp). Use this selectively — it adds a build/runtime layer, so reserve it for skills running model-generated or third-party code. (5) ONE HOST CLIENT, MANY TRANSPORTS-READY: build the host's MCP client so stdio is the default for local skills but the same client abstraction can later target Streamable HTTP for remote skills (Streamable HTTP replaced SSE as the recommended remote transport in spec 2025-03-26). NET: MCP-stdio child-process-per-skill + JSON-Schema-from-native-types + manifest/registry discovery + optional WASM/WIT inner sandbox is the recommended architecture; it directly maps onto Local-Claw's TS MCP server / Python MCP client / polyglot skill subprocess design.

pitfalls: STDOUT CORRUPTION (the #1 stdio-skill killer). The stdio transport reserves stdout EXCLUSIVELY for JSON-RPC framing. ANY non-protocol write to stdout — Python print()/logging to stdout, Node console.log(), Rust println!/dbg!, a dependency that prints a banner, ANSI color codes, an emoji in a log line — interleaves with the JSON-RPC stream and breaks the host's parser. Symptoms are misleading: 'Parse error: Unexpected token', 'JSON Parse error: Unexpected identifier Server', or 'Method not found: notifications/initialized'. ENFORCE stderr-only logging in every skill (Python: logging.StreamHandler(sys.stderr) and never bare print; Node: console.error; Rust: eprintln!/tracing to stderr) and lint/test for stray stdout writes. Confirmed across multiple real-world MCP issues (dirmacs/daedra#4, ruvnet/claude-flow#835, codewithmukesh/dotnet-claude-kit#10) and the official MCP debugging docs.

COLD-START LATENCY PER CALL. Spawning a fresh subprocess (and re-importing Python, booting a Node V8 isolate, or initializing a Rust binary) on EVERY tool call taxes ~100-400ms+ of pure process/runtime startup before any work happens. Anti-pattern: spawn-per-invocation. Fix: keep one warm, long-lived subprocess per skill, reused across calls, with the MCP session (initialize handshake + cached tools/list) established once at registration and held open. Only restart on crash or hot-reload.

SCHEMA DRIFT. Hand-authored tool schemas (declared at registration) silently diverge from the skill's actual runtime parameter handling as the code evolves, so the host validates against a stale contract and the model gets misled. NEVER hand-write JSON Schema — generate it from the native types (Zod/Standard Schema in TS, pydantic .model_json_schema() in Python, schemars derive in Rust) so the schema and the executed code share one source of truth. Treat tools/list output as the live, authoritative schema, not a copy stored in the manifest.

SELF-CONTAINED SCHEMA VIOLATION (external $ref). MCP tool inputSchema/outputSchema must be SELF-CONTAINED JSON Schema — they cannot reference external documents or files via $ref. Generators that emit $ref pointing at a sibling file/URL, or that leave dangling $defs, produce schemas the host (and the model) cannot resolve. Inline all $defs/definitions into each tool schema (bundle/dereference before publishing) so every schema stands alone. This is a common foot-gun when reusing shared type libraries across skills.

RUNTIME VERSION SKEW. A skill built and tested against one Node/Python/Rust (or SDK) version is spawned by a host whose environment resolves a different interpreter/toolchain, causing import errors, ABI mismatches in native deps, or subtly different JSON serialization. Pin the runtime per skill in its manifest (and/or ship a lockfile / pinned venv / vendored binary), set the spawn command explicitly (don't rely on ambient PATH), and validate the skill's reported version against the manifest at registration.

CAPABILITY / TRUST CONFUSION. OS-process skills inherit FULL AMBIENT AUTHORITY — they run with the host user's filesystem, network, and env access — unlike a WASM/WASI component which is deny-by-default and only gets explicitly granted capabilities. Treating a subprocess skill as 'sandboxed' is a security mistake. Either explicitly constrain subprocess skills (restricted user, seccomp/landlock, scrubbed env, no inherited secrets, read-only cwd) or run untrusted/model-generated skills inside a WASM component (Wasmtime/Extism) where capabilities are granted, not assumed.

TOOL NAME COLLISIONS. MCP gives no built-in namespace isolation across skills, so two skills each exposing a tool named 'search' or 'run' collide in the flattened tool list presented to the model. Prefix every tool with an org/skill namespace (e.g. localclaw.fs.read, skillname__toolname) in the registry layer and resolve back to the owning subprocess on dispatch; never expose raw, unqualified tool names from multiple skills.

NO SUPERVISION. A skill subprocess that crashes, deadlocks, or hangs mid-call will block the host's agent loop indefinitely if there's no supervisor: a stuck call_tool await never returns and in-flight requests pile up. Wrap every call in a per-call timeout, detect dead processes (exit code / broken pipe / failed initialize), restart with backoff, and fail the specific tool call fast (returning an error result to the model) rather than letting one bad skill freeze the whole host.

WHAT THE CURRENT SPEC RISKS GETTING WRONG: relying on filesystem-convention scanning instead of an explicit manifest+registry; assuming process isolation equals security sandboxing; and not making warm-process reuse + supervision (timeout, crash-restart, stderr capture) first-class — these are the gaps most likely to surface as flaky skills in Local-Claw.

Feature: Register a TypeScript skill via MCP stdio
  As the Local-Claw host
  I want to spawn a TS skill as a child-process MCP server and discover its tools
  So that the agent can invoke them by name

  Scenario: Successful discovery of a TypeScript skill
    Given a skill manifest declaring command "node" and args ["skills/formatter/dist/server.js"] with language "typescript"
    And the skill logs only to stderr (no writes to stdout)
    When the host spawns the subprocess and opens an stdio MCP session
    And the host completes the initialize handshake and calls tools/list
    Then the response is valid JSON-RPC 2.0 with no parse errors
    And each returned tool has a name, description, and a self-contained inputSchema (no external $ref)
    And the host caches the tools under the namespace "formatter" and marks the skill READY
    And the warm subprocess remains alive for reuse across subsequent calls

Feature: Sandboxed Rust WASM skill invocation
  As the Local-Claw host
  I want untrusted Rust compute skills to run as capability-restricted WASM components
  So that a skill cannot touch the filesystem or network unless explicitly granted

  Scenario: WASM skill is denied filesystem access by default
    Given a Rust skill compiled to a WASI Preview 2 component described by a WIT interface
    And the skill is loaded into a Wasmtime/Extism runtime behind an MCP server with NO preopened directories and NO network capability
    When the agent calls the skill's "transform" tool with valid input
    Then the tool returns its computed result successfully
    But when the skill attempts to open a file on the host filesystem
    Then the attempt fails with a capability/permission error inside the sandbox
    And the host process and other skills are unaffected

Feature: Schema validation gate before subprocess dispatch
  As the Local-Claw host
  I want inputs validated against the skill's advertised JSON Schema before calling the subprocess
  So that malformed tool calls are rejected without spending a round-trip or risking the skill

  Scenario: Bad input is rejected before the subprocess call
    Given a registered skill whose tool "resize_image" requires integer fields "width" and "height"
    And the host has cached that tool's self-contained inputSchema from tools/list
    When the agent issues a call with width="big" (a string) and no height
    Then the host validates the arguments against the cached JSON Schema and the validation FAILS
    And the host returns a structured validation error to the agent
    And no tools/call request is ever sent to the skill subprocess

Feature: Hot-reload a skill without dropping in-flight requests
  As the Local-Claw host
  I want to swap a skill's subprocess to a new version gracefully
  So that running tool calls finish and new calls hit the new version

  Scenario: Drain-and-swap on hot-reload
    Given a skill "summarizer" is READY with two tool calls currently in flight
    When a new version of the summarizer is published and a reload is requested
    Then the host marks the old subprocess DRAINING and stops routing new calls to it
    And the two in-flight calls are allowed to complete and return normally
    And the host spawns the new-version subprocess, runs initialize + tools/list, and validates the version against the manifest
    And once the new subprocess is READY the old one is shut down cleanly
    And no in-flight request was cancelled or lost during the swap
optimal_implementation:
Implement a Python SkillRegistry that spawns each skill as a warm, long-lived MCP stdio subprocess via the official `mcp` SDK, caches tools/list, namespaces + routes tool calls, enforces per-call timeouts, and supervises crashes with restart/backoff. Sketch:

```python
import asyncio, logging, sys, time
from contextlib import AsyncExitStack
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

log = logging.getLogger("skillregistry")  # configure handler -> sys.stderr ONLY

@dataclass
class SkillManifest:
    name: str            # namespace prefix, e.g. "formatter"
    command: str         # "node" | "python" | absolute path to rust binary
    args: list[str]
    env: dict | None = None
    version: str | None = None
    language: str | None = None

@dataclass
class SkillProcess:
    manifest: SkillManifest
    session: ClientSession | None = None
    stack: AsyncExitStack | None = None
    tools: dict[str, dict] = field(default_factory=dict)  # tool_name -> inputSchema
    state: str = "INIT"                                    # INIT|READY|DRAINING|DEAD
    inflight: int = 0
    restarts: int = 0

class SkillRegistry:
    def __init__(self, call_timeout: float = 30.0):
        self._skills: dict[str, SkillProcess] = {}
        self._tool_index: dict[str, str] = {}   # "ns.tool" -> skill name
        self._call_timeout = call_timeout
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def register(self, m: SkillManifest) -> None:
        sp = SkillProcess(manifest=m)
        await self._spawn(sp)            # start warm subprocess + initialize + cache tools/list
        self._skills[m.name] = sp

    async def _spawn(self, sp: SkillProcess) -> None:
        m = sp.manifest
        params = StdioServerParameters(command=m.command, args=m.args, env=m.env)
        stack = AsyncExitStack()
        read, write = await stack.enter_async_context(stdio_client(params))
        session = await stack.enter_async_context(ClientSession(read, write))
        await session.initialize()                              # MCP handshake (once, kept warm)
        listed = await session.list_tools()
        sp.session, sp.stack, sp.tools, sp.state = session, stack, {}, "READY"
        for t in listed.tools:                                   # cache live, authoritative schema
            qualified = f"{m.name}.{t.name}"                     # namespace -> no collisions
            sp.tools[t.name] = t.inputSchema
            self._tool_index[qualified] = m.name
        if m.version and getattr(listed, "version", None):       # optional version-skew guard
            ...  # compare/log mismatch

    async def call_tool(self, qualified_name: str, arguments: dict) -> object:
        ns, _, tool = qualified_name.partition(".")
        sp = self._skills.get(ns)
        if sp is None or sp.state == "DEAD":
            raise SkillUnavailable(qualified_name)
        validate(arguments, sp.tools[tool])  # jsonschema gate BEFORE dispatch; raises on bad input
        sp.inflight += 1
        try:
            return await asyncio.wait_for(                       # per-call timeout
                sp.session.call_tool(tool, arguments),
                timeout=self._call_timeout,
            )
        except (asyncio.TimeoutError, Exception) as e:
            log.error("call %s failed: %r", qualified_name, e)   # -> stderr
            asyncio.create_task(self._maybe_restart(sp))         # supervision trigger
            raise
        finally:
            sp.inflight -= 1

    async def _maybe_restart(self, sp: SkillProcess) -> None:
        async with self._lock:
            if sp.state == "DEAD":
                return
            sp.state = "DEAD"
            for q in [k for k, v in self._tool_index.items() if v == sp.manifest.name]:
                self._tool_index.pop(q, None)
            if sp.stack:
                await sp.stack.aclose()
            backoff = min(2 ** sp.restarts, 30)
            sp.restarts += 1
            await asyncio.sleep(backoff)                          # exponential backoff
            await self._spawn(sp)                                 # re-cache tools/list on restart

    async def supervise(self, interval: float = 5.0) -> None:    # background health loop
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(interval)
            for sp in list(self._skills.values()):
                if sp.session is None or not _process_alive(sp):
                    await self._maybe_restart(sp)
```

Key rules baked in: (1) one warm subprocess per skill, initialize + tools/list run once and reused (no spawn-per-call); (2) the cached inputSchema comes from tools/list, never hand-authored; (3) jsonschema validation gates dispatch so bad input never reaches the subprocess; (4) every call is wrapped in asyncio.wait_for for a per-call timeout; (5) crashes/timeouts trigger _maybe_restart with exponential backoff and a background supervise() loop catches dead processes; (6) tools are namespaced (ns.tool) to avoid collisions; (7) ALL logging goes to sys.stderr so the host's own stdout is never polluted (and skill subprocesses must do the same). For hot-reload: add a reload(name) that sets state=DRAINING, waits while sp.inflight>0, spawns the new version, then aclose()s the old stack — draining in-flight calls before swap.
sota_improvements: WASM Component Model + WIT as the long-term skill target. Move performance/untrusted skills from OS subprocesses to WASI Preview 2 components described by WIT interfaces, run in Wasmtime (or via Extism). Benefits over subprocess-MCP: portable single-artifact distribution, near-native speed, deterministic resource caps, and true capability sandboxing — while still fronted by an MCP server so the agent sees no difference (the hyper-mcp 'MCP outside, WASM inside' pattern).

Streamable HTTP transport for remote/cloud skills. Keep stdio as the local default but build the host client transport-agnostic so the same registry can mount remote skills over Streamable HTTP (the MCP-recommended remote transport since spec 2025-03-26, replacing SSE). This lets heavy or GPU-bound skills run off-box without changing the agent-facing contract.

Versioned registry with semver resolution and side-by-side major versions. Extend the manifest/registry to carry semver and resolve skills by version range, allowing two incompatible major versions of a skill to run simultaneously (skillname@1 and skillname@2 as distinct namespaces). This neutralizes runtime-version skew and lets skills upgrade without a flag-day migration.

Capability-based security, deny-by-default. Stop treating subprocess skills as trusted. Adopt a WASI-style explicit grant model: a skill declares the capabilities it needs (specific paths, network hosts, env keys) in its manifest, and the host grants nothing else — enforced natively for WASM skills and via OS confinement (restricted user, seccomp/landlock, scrubbed env) for subprocess skills.

Schema-first codegen instead of hand-written per-language clients. Generate client bindings and the host's typed call surface from a single source of truth (WIT for WASM skills, JSON Schema / OpenAPI for MCP skills) rather than hand-writing a client per language. This kills schema drift at the source and makes adding a fourth language (e.g. Go) a code-generation step, not a re-implementation.
